claims.claim: The documented runtime interceptor clear method is absent from AxiosInterceptorManager types.
claims.reason: README explicitly calls both clear methods. The runtime manager implements clear, while the complete declared interface contains only use/eject; the request/response interceptor properties are typed by that interface. TypeScript cannot resolve clear on those declared properties. This is a type/API mismatch, not a missing runtime implementation.

claims.claim: Default callable AxiosInstance overloads wrap the response type twice.
claims.reason: AxiosPromise<T> is Promise<AxiosResponse<T>>. Substituting the callable default R=AxiosResponse<T> into AxiosPromise<R> yields the nested response, whereas Axios.request returns Promise<R>. Runtime createInstance binds request, so callable and method returns share the runtime shape. The declared data type therefore differs from that runtime contract.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: export type AxiosPromise<T = any> = Promise<AxiosResponse<T>>;

claims.claim: extend can mutate an ordinary destination prototype through an own enumerable __proto__ source key.
claims.reason: forEach admits own enumerable keys and extend assigns their values without filtering. An object-valued own __proto__ data property reaches the inherited setter on an ordinary destination. This is target-local mutation, not global Object.prototype pollution. Selected createInstance calls copy Axios.prototype and a constructed context, so an external untrusted request exploit is not established and receives no credit.

claims.claim: Malformed numeric array-like lengths can throw RangeError rather than return null.
claims.reason: Only numeric type is checked before Array(length); negative, fractional, non-finite or above-maximum array lengths violate the constructor contract. toFormData reaches this helper for an object-valued top-level [] field; the public toFormData export makes that path available. Valid ordinary arrays bypass this allocation. This is the malformed-length failure, not proof of resource exhaustion.

claims.claim: Large accepted lengths can exhaust memory or other application resources.
claims.reason: Array(length) may allocate sparse storage; source alone does not establish engine allocation strategy, failure threshold or an attacker-controlled application entry. The copy loop scales with length, but no controlled resource reproduction or explicit resource budget is supplied. The invalid-length exception is scored separately.

claims.claim: A matching non-global or non-advancing zero-width regex can make matchAll loop forever.
claims.reason: The helper repeats exec and pushes every match without checking flags or progress. A matching non-global regex repeats the same result; a global zero-width match need not advance lastIndex. This proves the helper-level conditional nontermination under those arguments.

claims.claim: An own __proto__ property passes the merged-name guard and mutates the destination prototype.

A custom object supplied as request data reaches classification in transformRequest. claims.claim: A null transitional options value reaches Object.keys(null) and throws native TypeError instead of the intended AxiosError.
claims.reason: The only selected assertOptions caller checks transitional !== undefined, which admits null. mergeConfig preserves a null source value. The validator accepts typeof null as object, then calls Object.keys. No earlier null guard resolves this path. This is invalid-input error classification, not an accepted valid null option.

claims.claim: If Symbol is unavailable and the FormData capability check is reached, direct Symbol access throws.
claims.reason: isSpecCompliant directly reads Symbol.toStringTag. Reach requires a truthy _Blob plus a truthy candidate with a function append method; the _Blob && guard can otherwise skip this function. An explicitly supplied Blob option can make the check reachable. This is a conditional compatibility fact only.

claims.claim: The Symbol access breaks a supported unpolyfilled serialization runtime.
claims.reason: README lists IE11 but does not establish exact polyfills, Blob/FormData capabilities, bundling or the deployed environment. _Blob short-circuiting also narrows reachability. No authorized runtime reproduction establishes a supported no-Symbol configuration, so the compatibility-impact allegation remains unresolved.

claims.claim: A constructor response header is combined with an inherited value instead of being preserved.
claims.reason: XHR sends raw response headers to parseHeaders. Lowercasing preserves constructor; parsed={} inherits a truthy constructor, so line 47 concatenates the inherited function representation with the supplied value on its first occurrence. __proto__ is another collision, but this does not prove global pollution or downstream exploitation.

claims.claim: Node GET data-URI decoding returns a payload without enforcing the configured finite maxContentLength.
claims.reason: The full data URI is decoded to Buffer in fromDataURI. The HTTP adapter data branch returns before HTTP stream accounting and performs no maxContentLength check. maxContentLength is documented as a Node response-size limit, so a finite limit can be exceeded by decoded data. Both reports share the same unbounded data-URI path and count once. The source establishes the bypass, not process exhaustion.

claims.claim: A FormData name __proto__[polluted] can cause formDataToJSON to write Object.prototype.polluted.
claims.reason: The fixed regex accepts __proto__ and polluted as path segments. At the first segment obj.__proto__ is Object.prototype, which is truthy and passes isObject, so no replacement array is created. Recursion writes the final property on that shared prototype. The method is exposed by axios.formToJSON for valid iterable FormData and also used by JSON FormData transformation. A fresh nonexisting polluted key suffices; no remote application entry is inferred.

claims.claim: Untrusted cookie metadata can alter browser cookie scope or security attributes.
claims.reason: write concatenates raw name/path/domain into document.cookie and escapes only the value. This verifies the string construction. However, no selected caller invokes write, and no supplied application trust boundary or authorized browser reproduction establishes interpretation of injected attributes, their precedence, domain acceptance or an actual scope/security change. The complete claimed security consequence remains Unknown; the string-concatenation observation is not separately credited as a defect.

claims.claim: An unescaped cookie name can alter matching or throw on malformed regex syntax.
claims.reason: The browser helper concatenates name directly into RegExp. A name containing an unmatched [ makes pattern construction fail; a regex metacharacter such as . broadens lookup. XHR supplies config.xsrfCookieName after the standard-browser and origin/credentials checks. This is a conditional helper/config correctness issue; attacker control of application configuration is not established.

claims.claim: Silent malformed-JSON handling returns the original string instead of the documented null.
claims.reason: The README explicitly promises null on parsing failure. With responseType=json and silentJSONParsing=true, the SyntaxError is suppressed because strictJSONParsing is false; transformResponse falls through to return data. The default forced parsing path also retains its original string on failure. No null assignment exists in this transform.

claims.claim: Logging the documented toJSON result can disclose Authorization values retained in request config.
claims.reason: AxiosError keeps the config and toJSON returns it without redaction. README documents Authorization defaults and directly logging error.toJSON(). On an ordinary error carrying such a header, the logged object therefore includes that header. This conditional documented-flow exposure is supported; it does not prove a specific application logged secrets, remote exfiltration or any particular logging infrastructure.

claims.claim: A throwing synchronous fulfillment handler with no rejection callback is replaced by TypeError.
claims.reason: use stores the callback as supplied, and README explicitly demonstrates null rejection with synchronous:true. The synchronous catch unconditionally calls onRejected outside a protecting catch. Thus a thrown fulfillment error is replaced by invoking null/undefined. Both returned findings describe the same cause and count once. Asynchronous chains use Promise.then and are a separate control.

claims.claim: The generated XHR cancellation-error branch reads undefined req and interrupts rejection/abort cleanup.
claims.reason: The adapter declares request, never req. A later active-request AbortSignal event with truthy type evaluates new CanceledError(...,req), throwing before reject and request.abort. Public dispatch rejects an initially aborted signal before adapter entry; the later signal event still reaches this defect. A normal CancelToken object without type takes the other branch, so not every cancellation is affected. Both findings share this cause. For asynchronous signal events the exception is not automatically the request promise rejection; the intended rejection can be bypassed and the request may stay active.

claims.claim: A stateful params serializer failure can reject yet allow request creation and sending to continue.
claims.reason: The reject wrapper sets rejected=true but the construction/send path never checks it. The first buildURL exception is caught without return, then options.path calls it again. Network activity can begin after rejection has been issued; actual wall-clock delivery order to a catch consumer is not asserted.

limitations: Independent adjudication of this successful new Review only; earlier adjudications supplied format context, never verdict input.
Exact source citations and helper-local conditional defects do not establish remote attacker reach or whole-system exploitability.
Operational resource-exhaustion, cookie security impact and supported no-Symbol runtime regression remain Unknown without authorized reproduction.
No upstream code/dependencies/tests were executed or installed; no network, provider, app, approval, retry, fallback or production mutations were performed.
This is one completed Review in a fixed five-case/seven-occurrence benchmark. A successful case cannot certify partial benchmark acceptance.

mitigationSuggestions.action: Require candidate dangerous keys to be traced through every selected guard. Add evaluator counterexamples for ordinary-object membership checks that accidentally block a proposed mutation while causing a different omission. Keep source truth and security consequence separate.

Preserve explicit uncertainty for resource budgets, application attacker entry and browser effects. Establish caller argument provenance and a supported contract before promoting a helper fact into a system exploit. Add safe-caller and bounded-runtime negative controls; do not run imported upstream code in the adjudicator.

Include complete short-circuit guards and an explicit supported runtime capability matrix before compatibility-impact claims. Retain conditional source behavior separately from unverified environment impact.

Investigate why the validated bounded sweep and HTTP technical domain rows miss a concrete selected cross-adapter configuration inconsistency despite inspecting both files. Strengthen generic contract comparison and branch-specific diagnostics using independent fixtures. Keep this registered gold and oracle out of product prompts and model inputs.
